title: How Hackers Stole $6.3 Billion from Binance, and Why Half Got Frozen
importance_reason: public: Lino's YouTube channel, about a theft four days old that is still being investigated, with named companies, a named state and named people; a viewer may repeat any number, and a claim stronger than the sources is unfair to Binance, to the firms that traced it, or to the viewer
audience: A curious viewer on YouTube, a developer or someone who has never held crypto, who saw the headline that Binance lost $6 billion. After watching, they can say where the money was (hot wallets), how the attackers got Binance's own system to sign (a laptop, a service container, fifty pre-signed notes), why about half was frozen and the rest could not be (stablecoins have an issuer with an off switch, bitcoin and ether do not), who is blamed, what is known and not known about AI's part, and who is paying.

youtube.title: How Hackers Stole $6.3 Billion from Binance, and Why Half Got Frozen (Explained by Opus 5.5)
alternatives: The Biggest Crypto Heist Ever: How Binance Lost $6.3 Billion
Fifty Signatures: The $6.3 Billion Binance Hack, Explained
description: On October 29, about $6.3 billion left Binance's hot wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes. Within hours, about half of it was frozen. The FBI says North Korea's TraderTraitor unit did it.

I had Opus 5.5 explain how it worked: where the money sat, how fifty notes signed by Binance's own hot wallet were prepared ahead of time so one would fit, why the stablecoins could be frozen and the bitcoin and ether couldn't, what is known and not known about AI's part, and who is paying. Status as of November 2, 2026. Binance's technical post-mortem was not out yet, so a few answers are still open, and the video says which.

I made this video with ShipShow, my open-source toolkit of skills and plugins that lets AI agents build narrated videos like this one, end to end. The narrator is an invented voice, not a real person. https://github.com/latent-variable/shipshow
